q: Biodiversity comes from two words; Bio means life and diversity means variability.
e: This is the exact definition provided in the textbook introduction.

q: The term 'Biodiversity' was coined by Edward O. Wilson in 1985.
e: The term 'Biodiversity' was coined by Walter G. Rosen in 1985.

q: Edward O. Wilson is now known as 'Father of Biodiversity'.
e: Edward O. Wilson popularized the term and is known as the Father of Biodiversity.

q: The term 'biodiversity' refers to the variety and variability among living organisms and the ecological complexes in which they occur.
e: This is the standard definition of biodiversity given in the text.

q: Biodiversity can be defined as the totality of genes, species and ecosystem of a region.
e: This encompasses the three main levels of biodiversity.

q: Biodiversity is usually taken to include diversity at four levels.
e: Biodiversity is usually taken to include diversity at three levels: ecosystem, species, and genetic.

q: An ecosystem is a community of organisms and their physical environment interacting each other's together.
e: This is the textbook definition of an ecosystem.

q: The diversity of ecological complexity includes variations in ecological niches, trophic structure, food-webs and nutrient cycling.
e: These are the components that make up ecosystem diversity.

q: Species diversity is defined as the number of species and abundance of each species that lives in a particular location.
e: This correctly defines species diversity.

q: The number of species in a community is known as species evenness.
e: The number of species in a community is known as species richness.

q: Species diversity not only considers richness, but also includes a measure of the evenness of the abundance of the different species.
e: Species diversity incorporates both species richness and evenness.

q: Coral reefs have a very high biodiversity; such an ecosystem offers many different ecological niches.
e: Coral reefs are cited as an example of an ecosystem with very high biodiversity.

q: Ecosystems with high species diversity tend to be less stable than ones with limited diversity.
e: Ecosystems with high species diversity tend to be more stable and better able to resist changes.

q: Genetic diversity refers to the variety of genetic information contained in all of the individual plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms.
e: This is the broad definition of genetic diversity.

q: Genetic diversity is the variety of genes between different species.
e: Genetic diversity is the variety of genes within a species.

q: The genetic differences between populations of the same species exist because populations may be adapted slightly differences in different parts of their ranges.
e: Local adaptations cause genetic differences between populations of the same species.

q: Genetic diversity is important in providing populations with the ability to adapt to changes in biotic and abiotic factors.
e: Genetic diversity gives populations the adaptive capacity to survive environmental changes.

q: Biodiversity is very important for the well-being of our planet, human health, food security, economy and livelihoods.
e: These are the key areas where biodiversity provides critical importance.

q: Rich biodiversity allows large-scale ecosystems to function and self-regulate.
e: Interdependence among organisms allows rich ecosystems to self-regulate.

q: If biodiversity is reduced in one area, the natural balance may be destroyed elsewhere.
e: Ecosystems are interlinked on a large scale across the earth.

q: Healthy ecosystem and rich biodiversity will increase ecosystem productivity.
e: Each species has a specific niche and role, increasing overall productivity.

q: Each species in an ecosystem has a specific niche which is a role to play.
e: A niche is the specific role a species plays in its ecosystem.

q: Rich biodiversity reduces the variety of crops by supporting a smaller number of plant species.
e: Rich biodiversity supports a larger number of plant species and a greater variety of crops.

q: Rich biodiversity contributes to climate stability.
e: Climate stability is listed as one of the benefits of a healthy ecosystem.

q: Rich biodiversity slows recovery from natural disasters.
e: Rich biodiversity helps speed recovery from natural disasters.

q: Myanmar is the largest country in mainland Southeast Asia with a land area of 676,577 $km^2$.
e: This is the stated geographic fact about Myanmar's size.

q: Myanmar has a large latitudinal range of 2,100 km.
e: The large latitudinal range contributes to the country's biological diversity.

q: Forests cover ranges from moist tropical rain forests in the north, through dry deciduous forests in central areas to temperate broad leaf and alpine forests toward the south.
e: Forests range from moist tropical rain forests in the south to temperate broad leaf and alpine forests toward the north.

q: Forest ecosystems are a carbon sink and stabilize soils.
e: These are key ecological functions of forest ecosystems.

q: By slowing water flow due to increased infiltration, forests help regulates the seasonal flow of water downstream.
e: Forests help recharge groundwater and regulate downstream water flow.

q: Forest constitutes the dominant vegetation type in Myanmar.
e: Forest is the dominant vegetation type, covering 43% of the total land area.

q: The total area of forest is 290,410 $km^2$ which is 43% of the total land area.
e: This is the exact statistic provided for forest cover in Myanmar.

q: All of the forest area in Myanmar is described as closed forest.
e: Only half of the forest area is described as closed forest, whereas the other half is 'open' or 'degraded'.

q: Dry forest occurs where rainfall is usually less than 400 mm a year.
e: Dry forests are characterized by low annual rainfall of less than 400 mm.

q: Mixed Deciduous Forest makes up 38% of Forest Areas in Myanmar.
e: This is the largest percentage among the forest types listed.

q: Hill and Temperate Evergreen Forest makes up 16% of Forest Areas in Myanmar.
e: Hill and Temperate Evergreen Forest makes up 25% of Forest Areas.

q: Tropical Evergreen Forest makes up 16% of Forest Areas in Myanmar.
e: Tropical Evergreen Forest accounts for 16% of the forest areas.

q: Dry Forest makes up 10% of Forest Areas in Myanmar.
e: Dry Forest accounts for 10% of the forest areas.

q: Deciduous Dipterocarp (Indaing) Forest makes up 5% of Forest Areas in Myanmar.
e: Deciduous Dipterocarp Forest accounts for 5% of the forest areas.

q: The International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) publishes the Red Data Book.
e: The IUCN is the organization responsible for the Red Data Book.

q: The red data symbolizes the warning signal for those species which are abundant and thriving.
e: The red data symbolizes the warning signal for endangered species likely to become extinct.

q: About 250 mammal species, more than 1,000 birds, 370 reptiles and 7,000 plants are recorded in Myanmar.
e: These are the recorded biodiversity statistics for Myanmar.

q: Among the recorded species in Myanmar, 39 species of mammals are globally threatened.
e: 39 mammal species are listed as globally threatened in Myanmar.

q: Among the recorded species in Myanmar, 45 species of reptiles are globally threatened.
e: 21 species of reptiles and 45 species of birds are globally threatened.

q: Dipterocarpus alatus is commonly known as the Gurjum tree and its IUCN Status is Endangered.
e: This is the correct common name and IUCN status for Dipterocarpus alatus.

q: Swietenia macrophylla is commonly known as Mahogany and its IUCN Status is Critically Endangered.
e: The IUCN Status of Swietenia macrophylla (Mahogany) is Endangered, not Critically Endangered.

q: Paphiopedilum wardii is commonly known as Black Orchid and its IUCN Status is Critically Endangered.
e: Black Orchid is correctly listed as Critically Endangered.

q: Elephas maximus is commonly known as the Asian Elephant and its IUCN Status is Endangered.
e: The Asian Elephant is correctly listed as Endangered.

q: Rucervus eldii thamin is commonly known as Eld's Deer and its IUCN Status is Critically Endangered.
e: The IUCN Status of Eld's Deer (Shwe Thamin) is Endangered.

q: Orcaella brevirostris is commonly known as the Irrawaddy Dolphin and its IUCN Status is Endangered.
e: The Irrawaddy Dolphin is correctly listed as Endangered.

q: Geochelone platynota is commonly known as the Burmese Star Tortoise and its IUCN Status is Critically Endangered.
e: The Burmese Star Tortoise is correctly listed as Critically Endangered.

q: Pavo muticus is commonly known as the Green Peafowl and its IUCN Status is Endangered.
e: The Green Peafowl is correctly listed as Endangered.

q: Cephalotaxus mannii is commonly known as Mann's plum yew and its IUCN Status is Endangered.
e: Mann's plum yew is correctly listed as Endangered.

q: Rhododendron arboreum is commonly known as Rhododendron and its IUCN Status is Critically Endangered.
e: The IUCN Status of Rhododendron arboreum is Endangered, not Critically Endangered.

q: Myanmar spans a vast area and has diverse geographical features and climates from tropical coral reefs to alpine habitats.
e: This highlights the extreme geographical and climatic diversity of Myanmar.

q: More than 3 billion people depend on marine and coastal biodiversity.
e: This is the stated global dependence on marine and coastal biodiversity.

q: More than 1.6 billion people rely on forests for their livelihoods.
e: This is the stated global dependence on forest biodiversity.

q: The loss of biodiversity affects the lives of more than 1 billion people living in dry lands.
e: Biodiversity loss severely impacts populations in dry lands.

q: There are five major threats to biodiversity.
e: The textbook lists exactly five major threats to biodiversity.

q: Habitat destruction has played a key role in extinction.
e: Habitat destruction is identified as a primary driver of extinction.

q: When habitats become divided into small areas, this is known as habitat aggregation.
e: When habitats become divided into small areas, this is known as habitat fragmentation.

q: Physically larger species and those living at lower latitudes or in forests or oceans are more sensitive to reduction in habitat area.
e: Larger species and those in specific biomes are highly sensitive to habitat loss.

q: Shifting cultivation in upland areas and gold mining are major reasons for habitat destruction in Myanmar.
e: These are specific examples of land-use change causing habitat destruction in Myanmar.

q: Pollution is caused by uncontrolled pesticide and herbicide uses, various factory wastes, and human sewage.
e: These are listed as primary causes of pollution threatening ecosystems.

q: Invasive alien species can be introduced unintentionally by tourists or through the transport of cargo.
e: Unintentional introduction is a common pathway for invasive alien species.

q: Genetic pollution indicates the gain of identity of wild plant species as a result of transfer of genes from crop plants.
e: Genetic pollution indicates the loss of identity of wild plant species due to gene transfer from crops.

q: Gene flow is expected to have its greatest effect on weed species that are closely related to crop plants.
e: Weeds closely related to crops are most susceptible to genetic pollution via gene flow.

q: The introduction of genetically engineered organisms into the complex ecosystems of our environment is considered a safe global experiment.
e: The introduction of genetically engineered organisms is considered a dangerous global experiment.

q: Overexploitation applies to natural resources such as water aquifers, grazing pastures and forests.
e: These are examples of natural resources subject to overexploitation.

q: Overfishing is the removal of a species of fish from a body of water at a rate greater than that the species can replenish its population naturally.
e: This is the exact definition of overfishing.

q: Overlogging is a form of overexploitation caused by legal or illegal logging activities that lead to sustainable deforestation.
e: Overlogging leads to unsustainable or irrecoverable deforestation.

q: Overhunting threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates.
e: One-third of endangered vertebrates are threatened specifically by overhunting.

q: Excluding edible fish, the illegal trade in wildlife is valued at $10 billion per year.
e: This is the stated financial value of the illegal wildlife trade.

q: As of 2016, 301 terrestrial mammals were threatened with extinction due to hunting for bushmeat.
e: This is the specific statistic provided regarding bushmeat hunting.

q: Bushmeat provides increased opportunity for transmission of several zoonotic viruses from animal hosts to humans, such as Ebola virus and HIV.
e: Bushmeat hunting is linked to the transmission of zoonotic diseases.

q: Climate change alters the climate patterns and ecosystems in which species have evolved and on which they depend.
e: Climate change disrupts the evolutionary environments of species.

q: Rising ocean temperatures and diminishing Arctic sea ice affects marine biodiversity and can shift vegetation zones.
e: These are specific impacts of climate change on global biodiversity.

q: An increase in the world's population will cause additional strains on resources.
e: Human overpopulation directly increases demand and strain on natural resources.

q: Wildlife trade refers to the commerce of products that are derived from domesticated animals or plants.
e: Wildlife trade refers to products derived from non-domesticated animals or plants.

q: Illegal wildlife trade contributes directly to the loss of species and habitat destruction.
e: Illegal trade is a direct driver of species loss and habitat degradation.

q: High demand from expanding illegal wildlife markets in neighboring countries is rapidly threatening the endangered wildlife of Myanmar.
e: Cross-border demand is a major threat to Myanmar's endangered species.

q: The most trafficked animal in the world is the tiger, accounting for as much as 20% of all illegal wildlife trade.
e: The pangolin is the most trafficked animal, accounting for 20% of illegal wildlife trade.

q: Pangolins are the only scaly mammal on earth.
e: Pangolins are uniquely characterized as the only scaly mammals.

q: In the last decade, more than one million pangolins were poached and killed for their scales.
e: This is the stated statistic for pangolin poaching over the last decade.

q: Wildlife smuggling may cause the introduction of invasive and harmful species into an ecosystem.
e: Smuggling can accidentally or intentionally introduce invasive species to new environments.

q: Outbreaks of zoonotic diseases including COVID-19 and H5N1 avian flu have been traced to live wildlife markets.
e: Live wildlife markets are linked to the emergence of zoonotic diseases.

q: CITES stands for the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna.
e: This is the correct full name of the CITES convention.

q: The Conservation of Biodiversity and Protected Areas Law was enacted in Myanmar in 2018.
e: This law was enacted in 2018 for wildlife protection in Myanmar.

q: Certain places in the world where wildlife trade is particularly threatening are called 'wildlife trade hotspots'.
e: This is the definition of wildlife trade hotspots.

q: Replacement of local landraces with modern varieties is a major threat to the agrobiodiversity of Myanmar.
e: Replacing local varieties reduces agricultural genetic diversity.

q: Factors causing habitat destruction include overpopulation, deforestation, pollution and global warming.
e: These are explicitly listed as factors causing habitat destruction.

q: Wind, rain, birds, bees, and insect pollinators have begun carrying genetically altered pollen into adjoining fields.
e: These natural vectors spread genetically altered pollen, causing genetic pollution.

q: Once released, it is very easy to recall genetically engineered organisms back to the laboratory or the field.
e: Once released, it is virtually impossible to recall genetically engineered organisms.

q: Overexploitation can lead to the destruction of the resource, as it will be unable to replenish.
e: Overharvesting outpaces the natural replenishment rate of resources.

q: An increase in population will inevitably create pressures leading to more deforestation and decreased biodiversity.
e: Population growth directly drives habitat loss and ecological degradation.

q: Much of demand for rhinoceros' horns and tiger bones arises out of the practice of traditional Chinese medicine.
e: Traditional medicine is a primary driver of demand for these specific animal parts.

q: Wildlife trade can involve the trade of living or dead individuals, tissues such as skins, bones, feathers, meat, or other products.
e: This broadly defines the scope of products involved in wildlife trade.

q: Poverty and a lack of alternative livelihoods aggravate the situation of illegal wildlife trade in Myanmar.
e: Socioeconomic factors like poverty drive local involvement in illegal trade.

q: Interspecific competition between species can be caused by wildlife smuggling introducing harmful species into an ecosystem.
e: Introduced species strain environmental resources through interspecific competition.

q: Climate change forces species to adjust, but many are not able to cope, causing them to become extinct.
e: Inability to adapt to rapid climate change leads to species extinction.

q: Conservation means keeping and protecting a living and changing environment.
e: This is the core definition of conservation provided in the text.

q: Active intervention is required to restore areas and to protect native species.
e: Conservation is an active process requiring management and intervention.

q: Narrowly Utilitarian reasons for conservation include ecosystem services like providing oxygen and pollinating crops.
e: Providing oxygen and pollinating crops are Broadly Utilitarian reasons; Narrowly Utilitarian involves direct products like food and drugs.

q: Broadly Utilitarian reasons for conservation include useful human products like food, fibres, drugs and medicines.
e: Food, fibres, and drugs are Narrowly Utilitarian; Broadly Utilitarian involves essential ecosystem services.

q: Ethical Utilitarian reasons for conservation state that every living species has an intrinsic value and every species has the right to live.
e: This defines the ethical moral obligation to conserve all species.

q: In situ methods are the ways of conservation of species which take place outside the natural habitat of the organism.
e: In situ methods take place in the natural habitat of the organism.

q: Maintaining the natural habitat means that all the 'life support systems' are provided.
e: Natural habitats inherently provide the necessary life support systems for species.

q: Nature reserves such as wildlife sanctuary, national park and biosphere reserve help endangered species by maintaining their habitat and genetic diversity.
e: These are examples of in situ conservation areas that protect habitats and genetics.

q: Keeping organisms in situ means putting them in the ecosystem where they belong.
e: In situ conservation keeps species in their native ecosystems.

q: Active management of nature reserves involves continuous monitoring and maintenance of effective boundaries.
e: These are key components of actively managing protected areas.

q: Ex situ methods are the ways to conserve animals and plants outside their natural habitats.
e: This is the correct definition of ex situ conservation.

q: Ex situ conservation methods are usually used as a first resort.
e: Ex situ conservation methods are usually used as a last resort when in situ is not possible.

q: In captive breeding programmes, individuals of an endangered species are bred in zoos and parks in an attempt to save the species from extinction.
e: This is the primary purpose of captive breeding programs.

q: The ultimate aim of captive breeding is to keep the captive-bred animals in the zoo permanently.
e: The ultimate aim is to reintroduce the captive-bred animals into the wild.

q: Artificial insemination and embryo transfer to a surrogate mother are techniques used in captive breeding programmes.
e: These are specific reproductive technologies used in captive breeding.

q: Cryogenics involves freezing eggs, sperm cells and embryos for future use.
e: Cryogenics is used to preserve genetic material for future breeding.

q: Keeping a pedigree is used in captive breeding to encourage inbreeding.
e: Keeping a pedigree is used to prevent inbreeding.

q: A problem with captive breeding is that there is not enough space or resources in zoos and parks for all the endangered species.
e: Limited space and resources are significant constraints for captive breeding.

q: Animals that have been bred in captivity may have problems adjusting to unsupported life in the wild.
e: Captive-bred animals often lack the survival skills needed for the wild.

q: It has been estimated that 25% of the world's flowering plant species could disappear within the next 50 years.
e: This is the stated projection for the loss of flowering plant species.

q: There are thought to be about 242,000 species of flowering plants now.
e: This is the estimated current number of flowering plant species.

q: Seeds in a seed bank are kept in warm, bright conditions to speed up the metabolism of the seed.
e: Seeds are kept in cold, dark conditions to slow down metabolism and prevent germination.

q: The storage of seeds is one of the most widespread and valuable ex situ approaches to conservation.
e: Seed banking is a highly effective and common ex situ method.

q: Seed banks protect and save plant genetic diversity.
e: Preserving seeds maintains the genetic diversity of plant species.

q: Saved and viable seeds contain useful genes that breeders can use for developing improved varieties of major food crops.
e: Seed banks serve as genetic reservoirs for agricultural improvement.

q: About 80,000 plant species are grown in private gardens, arboretums and botanical gardens all over the world.
e: This is the stated number of plant species cultivated in these ex situ locations.

q: Botanical gardens serve as taxonomic and systematic research centers.
e: Botanical gardens play a major role in scientific plant research.

q: One of the major objectives of botanical gardens is to create and support collections of native taxa.
e: Maintaining native plant collections is a core objective of botanical gardens.

q: Protected areas (PAs) are important tools for biodiversity conservation and sustainable development.
e: PAs are fundamental strategies for global conservation efforts.

q: Protected areas safeguard ecosystems and their services, such as water provision, food production, and carbon sequestration.
e: These are critical ecosystem services protected by PAs.

q: In Myanmar, 42 protected areas have been established.
e: This is the exact number of protected areas established in Myanmar.

q: Scientific reserves are held for the protection of their features for scientific study, research, education, and the benefit of the country.
e: This is the defined purpose of scientific reserves.

q: A national park is an area set aside by a national government for the preservation of the natural environment.
e: This is the standard definition of a national park.

q: In a national park, settlement and resource harvesting are strictly encouraged.
e: In a national park, no settlement or resource harvesting is allowed.

q: Visitors are permitted in a national park.
e: Unlike some strict reserves, visitors are permitted in national parks.

q: A marine national park is a permanent marine reservation for the conservation of species.
e: This defines the purpose of a marine national park.

q: Lampi Island Marine National Park is an example of a marine national park.
e: Lampi Island is cited as the example for marine national parks.

q: A nature reserve is a protected area of importance for flora, fauna, or features of geological or other special interest.
e: This is the definition of a nature reserve.

q: Popa Mountain Park and Hkakaborazi National Park are examples of nature reserves.
e: These are the specific examples given for nature reserves in the text.

q: A wildlife sanctuary is an area where animal habitats and their surroundings are protected from any sort of disturbance.
e: This defines the primary function of a wildlife sanctuary.

q: The capturing, killing and poaching of animals is strictly prohibited in wildlife sanctuaries.
e: Strict protection from hunting and poaching is enforced in sanctuaries.

q: Hlawga Park and Chatthin Wildlife Sanctuary are examples of wildlife sanctuaries.
e: These are the specific examples given for wildlife sanctuaries.

q: The Government of Myanmar introduced Community forest in the early 1990s.
e: The Community forest initiative was introduced in the early 1990s.

q: Community forest means all sustainable forest management and utilization activities, in which the local community itself is involved.
e: Local community involvement is the defining feature of Community forests.

q: Community forests are an important tool for biodiversity conservation and community-driven development.
e: Community forests serve dual purposes of conservation and local development.

q: Reintroduction programmes for captive-bred animals are always inexpensive and quick to complete.
e: Reintroduction programmes can be very expensive, time consuming, and may fail.

q: Ex situ conservation methods include captive breeding of animals, storage of seeds in the seed bank and cultivation of plants in botanical garden.
e: These are the three primary methods of ex situ conservation listed.

q: Restocking and reintroducing of once-common species from stocks produced by captive breeding programmes is part of active management of nature reserves.
e: Reintroduction is a key active management strategy for in situ reserves.

q: Tanintharyi Nature Reserve is given as an example of a scientific reserve in the textbook.
e: Tanintharyi Nature Reserve is explicitly listed under the scientific reserve category.
